text: Kikukawa Eizan studied first with his father Eiji, a minor painter of the Kanō school, and then with Suzuki Nanrei of the Shijō school. He may also have studied with Totoya Hokkei. In the 1830s he produced many woodblock prints of beautiful women, then gave up printmaking for painting. He was the most prolific, longest-lived and ultimately the best of the late followers of Utamaro who tried to carry on his bijin style. Do not confuse him with Harukawa Eizan.

By the later 15th century Rogier van der Weyden had eclipsed Jan van Eyck in popularity. His paintings were exported to Italy and Spain, and he took commissions from Philip the Good and other Burgundian nobles and foreign aristocrats. His surviving works are mainly religious triptychs and altarpieces, plus portraits and diptychs. He began as Roger de la Pasture. His fame lasted until the 17th century. By the mid-18th century he was almost forgotten.

Jan Bulthuis came from Groningen, where he trained under Jurriaan Andriessen as a painter and Johannes Wieringa as a draftsman. He painted landscapes at first, but later concentrated on townscapes and country views. From 1780 he worked in Amsterdam. In 1785 he enrolled at the Stadstekenacademie and won a gold medal there. He made a series of drawings for Adriaan Loosjes's description of the Zaan villages. He died in 1801.

Francesco Bassano the Younger studied with his father Jacopo and worked in the family workshop with his three brothers. He was the eldest son. Francesco moved to Venice, where he ran the branch of the family business, and he was commissioned to paint a series of historical pictures in the Doge's Palace. He was prone to hypochondria. That made his other ailments worse. He died in 1592.

Three separate blocks went into every print by Antonio da Trento: one for the outlines, one for the shadows, and one for the lighter tints. He specialized in chiaroscuro woodcuts, mostly of religious subjects. He probably learned wood engraving from Ugo da Carpi, and later followed Parmigianino and then the School of Fontainebleau. Three documented works are The Beheading of St. Peter and St. Paul, The Tiburtine Sibyl and Psyche Saluted by the People.

Jerome Myers worked briefly as an actor and scene painter before studying art for a year at Cooper Union and then eight years at the Art Students League, mainly with George de Forest Brush. Born in Petersburg, Virginia, he spent his adult life in New York City. He painted the city and its people with sympathy. He helped organize the 1913 Armory Show, which introduced European modernism to America. He also wrote.

Hardly any documents mention Hans Brosamer apart from his prints. He was probably born in Fulda in the late 1490s, was active there from 1536 to 1545, and later worked in Erfurt. His works include over 600 woodcuts, mostly book illustrations, and 38 engravings. Because his engravings are small, he counts among the Little Masters. He also painted half-length portraits of local elites. He died around 1554.

Giovanni Battista Vanni studied under Jacopo da Empoli, Aurelio Lomi and Matteo Rosselli, and then became a disciple of Cristofano Allori. He is better known as an engraver than as a painter. From 1624 to 1632 he lived in Rome, and he went back to Florence after visiting Venice. In 1642 he etched fifteen plates after Correggio's frescoes in the cupola of Parma Cathedral. He also engraved Veronese's Marriage at Cana.

At twenty Joseph Vivien left Lyon for Paris and found work in Charles Le Brun's large atelier. In 1701 the Académie royale accepted him as a pastel portraitist, and his reception pieces, pastel portraits of the sculptor François Girardon and the architect Robert de Cotte, are in the Louvre. He was made counsellor to the Academy and housed at the Gobelins. He visited Brussels and worked in Munich as first painter to a brother of the Elector of Cologne.

Adriaan de Lelie came from Tilburg and trained with A. Peeters, who painted ornaments, and then with Andreas Bernardus de Quertenmont in Antwerp. In Düsseldorf he copied many portraits by Rubens and Van Dyck. On Professor Camper's advice he settled in Amsterdam. He painted a great number of portraits and cabinet pictures, including one of the art lover Jan Gildemeester showing his collection to a party. His Drawing Academy of the Felix Meritis Society is one of his best.

In 1846 John Mix Stanley showed a gallery of 85 of his paintings in Cincinnati and Louisville. He grew up in the Finger Lakes region of New York and started by painting signs and portraits. In 1842 he went to the American West to paint Native American life. In the Mexican–American War he joined Colonel Kearney's expedition to California and painted the campaign, and later the Oregon Territory. A big exhibit followed at the Smithsonian. It held over 150 works.

Tawaraya Sōtatsu is best known for decorating calligraphic works by his partner Hon'ami Kōetsu. His folding screens are spectacular and highly influential, and two of them, Wind God and Thunder God, are National Treasures. He also painted the Sekiya and Miotsukushi chapters of The Tale of Genji. He popularized tarashikomi. In that technique a second layer of paint goes on before the first dries. With Kōetsu he is credited with co-founding the Rinpa school.

Pietro della Vecchia was once incorrectly called Pietro Muttoni. He worked in many genres between late Mannerism and early Baroque: altarpieces, portraits, genre scenes and grotesques. He also made pastiches of the leading Italian painters of the 16th century. He designed cartoons for mosaics and restored art, and collectors sought him out as an expert and for valuations of artworks. He lived mostly in Venice.

Very little documentation of Simone Martini's life survives, and art historians debate many attributions. He is thought to have been a pupil of Duccio. Vasari said he was a pupil of Giotto instead, and went with him to Rome. His brother-in-law was the artist Lippo Memmi, and Gombrich said he was a friend of Petrarch. He greatly influenced the International Gothic style. He came from Siena and died in 1344.
